questions.question: Read the passage on friendship, then answer: how are we separated from our families?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** We are separated from our families because today many of us **live and work at great distances from where we were born or grew up**, so we are **cut off from our original families**, and the pain we feel when we are away from them can be significant.

**What the passage says.**

> "Today many of us live and work at great distances from where we were born or we grew up and are separated from our original families. The pain we feel when we are away from our families can be significant."

**Why the passage begins here.** The separation is the premise of the whole argument: because the family is far away, friendship has taken over the "necessary human connection" it once provided, and friends now supply the intimacy and the sense of values that relatives used to.

questions.question: How does friendship grow?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Like watering a plant**, we grow our friendships — and all our relationships — **by nurturing them**. Friendships need the same attention as other relationships if they are to continue, and they can be "delightfully non-judgmental, supportive, understanding and fun".

**What the passage says.**

> "Like watering a plant, we grow our friendships (and all our relationships) by nurturing them."

**What nurturing means here.** The passage spells it out a little later: by **revealing yourself**, by **being attentive**, by **remembering what is most important to your friends and asking them about it**, by **putting yourself in their position** and by **showing empathy** — seeing the world through the eyes of your friends.

questions.question: How do communication skills grow?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Communication skills are **fundamental in all friendships**: **the more friends and acquaintances one has, the greater one's communication skills**. Some people therefore call these skills "people skills".

**What the passage says.**

> "The more friends and acquaintances one has, the greater one's communication skills. Some call these, people skills."

**Caution while answering.** The passage states the relation between the number of friends and the growth of communication skills; it does not give a list of techniques. Do not invent a list of "listening, speaking, writing" — the marks are for the relation the passage draws.

questions.question: Why is friendship considered an essential human need?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Because **the happiness of the individual relies on friendships, which form a necessary human connection**; it is perfectly normal to need and want friends, and **depression is more prevalent among those who lack friends**. Friends give the intimacy and richness of life that a lonely person misses.

**What the passage adds.** A friendship can bring out "the positive side that you never show in any other relationship", because the pressure of playing a "role" (daughter, partner or child) is removed. With a friend you can be yourself and are free to change, and you can "explain yourself to a friend openly without the fear of hurting a family member".

questions.question: How can friendship be continued?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Friendship can be continued by **using all the communication skills** — active listening, questioning, negotiation, reflecting content, reflecting emotion and editing yourself. In practice this means being considerate, showing empathy and accepting a person from a different family or cultural background.

**What the passage says.**

> "Friendships are made by being considerate which means all the communication skills into play: active listening skills, questioning skills, negotiation skills, reflecting content skills, reflecting emotion skill, and editing yourself."

**The deeper point.** Such acceptance "in turn we gain tolerance and acceptance for our own difference" — friendship is thus a training in living with people unlike ourselves.

questions.question: Pick out words from the passage which mean the same as each of the following: (i) basic essential (para-3) (ii) a trial performance (para-5).
questions.answer:
**Answer.** (i) basic essential — **fundamental**; (ii) a trial performance — **rehearsals**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "Communication skills are **fundamental** in all friendships."

> "...in friendships you get to have lots of **rehearsals** and discussion about changes as you experience them."

**Note.** Give one word for each; do not add a phrase, and keep the spelling of the passage.

questions.question: On the basis of your reading of the passage on happiness, make notes on it using headings and sub-headings, with recognizable abbreviations wherever necessary.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: The Way of Happiness**

1. **Happiness — a def. problem**
   1.1 no agreed def.
   1.2 commonly equated with fun, good living, plenty of money
   1.3 the rich, with luxuries & parties, are often unhappy

2. **Fun vs. happiness**
   2.1 fun — what we experience *during* an act
   2.2 happ. — an intangible something experienced *after* the act
   2.3 fun is fleeting; happ. is a stronger, deeper, more abiding emotion

3. **The way to happiness**
   3.1 happ. as the ultimate goal
   3.2 not a smooth highway; a rocky & rugged path
   3.3 needs effort — "roll up our sleeves"
   3.4 earned by great, constant effort, not in spurts

4. **Happiness & pain**
   4.1 fallacy: fun/pleasure = happ., so pain = unhapp.
   4.2 things that bring happ. involve some pain
   4.3 difficult endeavours — raising children, deep relationships, worthwhile work

5. **Happiness is not a permanent vacation**
   5.1 riches alone do not make one blissful
   5.2 work is worship; work gives confidence & self-worth
   5.3 job satisfaction > pay cheque
   5.4 basic shelter & food still necessary

**Key to abbreviations.** def. – definition; happ. – happiness; vs. – versus; e.g. – for example; & – and.

questions.question: Write a summary of the happiness passage in about 80 words and suggest a suitable title.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: Happiness — Earned, Not Given**

Happiness has no agreed definition; people wrongly equate it with fun, good living and money, yet the rich are often unhappy. Fun is what we experience during an act, happiness is the intangible something we feel after it, and it is deeper and more abiding. The way to happiness is a rocky path that demands effort, not a smooth highway, and things that bring happiness often involve pain. Nor is happiness a permanent vacation: work, not riches, gives confidence, self-worth and satisfaction.

**Word count.** About 100 words; cut the examples if a strict 80 is required.

questions.question: The Students' Council of your college has organised an education tour to New Delhi for students of Class XII. As the President of the Council, write a notice in not more than 40 words informing the students about this tour.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**ABC SCHOOL XYZ — NOTICE**

*2nd April 2018*

**EDUCATION TOUR TO NEW DELHI**

It is informed to all the students of Class XII that our college is going on an educational trip to Delhi on **5 April 2018 at 9 a.m.** Everyone will come with a lunch box and other valuable things. Interested students may give their names to the undersigned.

**Abijeet Kr. Sharma**
President of Council

**Format points.** The word NOTICE, the institution, the date, **what, when, where** and **whom to contact** — and no more than forty words in the body, since the limit is part of the question.

questions.question: You are the General Manager of B.C.C. Consultancy, Ramgarh. You want to appoint a lady receptionist for your firm. Give an advertisement to be published in the classified columns of a local daily.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**SITUATION VACANT**

**B.C.C. Consultancy, Ramgarh** requires a **lady receptionist** for its office. The candidate should have passed **Class 10 with 60% marks**, should be below 30 years, and must have a pleasant manner and a good command of Hindi and English. **Comfortable salary** for the right person; local candidates preferred.

Apply with a photograph to the **General Manager, B.C.C. Consultancy, Ramgarh**, within seven days.

**Format points.** A classified "Situation Vacant" carries a heading in capitals, the name of the firm and the post, the qualification and age, the salary and the address to apply to. Write no salutation and no letter — it is an advertisement, not an application.

questions.question: Your college celebrated the Republic Day with songs and cultural events. Write a report to be published in the college magazine.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**REPUBLIC DAY CELEBRATED IN COLLEGE**

*Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 26 January 2018.** Republic Day was celebrated by the staff and students of **XYZ College** with songs and a cultural event. **A. K. Sharma**, head of the educational board, hoisted the national flag and spoke to the gathering about the solemnity of the occasion and the role played by the constitutional makers, with particular reference to **Dr. B. R. Ambedkar**.

The college Principal, Padmaj, threw light on the various tasks to be undertaken by the present students, who are the future citizens of the country. Cultural activities were held and the gathering was treated to some spectacular musical feats. The Principal welcomed the chief guest, the distinguished invitees and the parents.

The chief guest said on the occasion that students should be brave and face all the challenges with courage, and asked them to be responsible in their role as good citizens. In the end all the students were given sweets to eat and the Principal gave a speech on how one can become a good citizen of the country.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the guests, the events in order, and the speeches summarised — all in the past tense and the third person.

questions.question: You are Prerna/Atul working for a local newspaper in Ranchi. Last week you attended a seminar on the importance of 'Blood Donation' organised by the Lions Club, Ranchi. Write a report on the seminar in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**BLOOD DONATION SEMINAR HELD**

*By Atul, Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 2 April 2018.** I attended a blood donation seminar-cum-camp in a school last Sunday, organised by the **Lions Club, Ranchi**. It was held in the school hall, and all the preparations — arrangement of beds, sanitation and so on — had been made in advance.

A team of doctors and nurses from the local government hospital had reached in time. The chief guest of the camp was the **SDO of the city**, who inaugurated the camp by cutting the ribbon. The students of our school and of other schools, besides the people of the city, were participating in the camp. After the formal registration I too was laid on a bed with a soft ball in my hand, and the process of extracting blood started; it took more than half an hour, and afterwards I was given fruit and milk along with the other donors.

The camp continued till 3.00 p.m. The chief guest then delivered a speech extolling those who had donated blood, and told the audience that the donated blood would be used for the lives of the injured and the sick.

**Format points.** A report of an event attended by the writer uses the first person only for the writer's own participation; the rest is in the third person and the past tense.

questions.question: Write a letter to the Editor of *The Express*, Ranchi, about the poor maintenance of the City Bus in your city, in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Examination Hall**
**Ranchi**
**2 April 2018**

The Editor
*The Express*
Ranchi

**Subject: Poor maintenance of city buses**

Sir

The buses running in the state of Ranchi tell a sad tale. It is a pity that even long-route buses are in a pitiable condition. The buses owned by the government are found, more often than not, in an ill-managed state. New buses put on the road give no complaint, but once a bus becomes a year or so old, its maintenance becomes a problem.

The windowpanes are found missing and in many cases they are found jammed. During winter or in the rainy season it becomes difficult to travel in such buses. Seats in some of the buses are in a bad shape. Through this letter I request the authorities to look into the matter and redress the grievances of the passengers.

Yours faithfully
**Alok Singh**

**Format points.** Sender's address and date, addressee, subject, the complaint with **specific evidence**, and a request for action.

questions.question: Write a letter to the Editor of *The Express*, Ranchi, complaining about the frequent breakdown in the supply of electricity in your village, in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Ashok Sharma**
Bariatu, Ranchi
Postal code: 834008
Phone no.: 91123456789
Date: 2 April 2018

The Editor
*The Express*
Morabadi, Ranchi

**Subject: Frequent breakdown in the supply of electricity in my village**

Sir

I would like to draw the attention of the authorities to the frequent breakdown of electricity in our locality. People have to face a lot of inconvenience due to the breakdown of electricity time and again. The whole area is thrown into darkness and the power supply is not restored for hours.

Students preparing for the examinations are the worst sufferers; they cannot concentrate on their studies. The weak and the old people suffer a lot when there is no electricity, and in summer the heat becomes unbearable without a fan. The matter was reported to the electricity department, but this is not the first time we have faced this problem.

I request you kindly to publish the above in the columns of your esteemed daily so that the higher authorities are compelled to initiate expeditious action.

Yours sincerely
**Ashok Sharma**

**Format points.** A letter of complaint names the **specific suffering of specific groups** — here students, the sick and the old — before it asks for action.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Child Labour' in about 200 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**CHILD LABOUR — A CHILDHOOD STOLEN**

Child labour takes place when children are forced to work at an age when they are expected to study and enjoy their phase of innocence. It implies lost or deprived childhood in various forms: mental, physical, social and sexual.

Not all children in India are lucky enough to enjoy their childhood. Many of them are forced to work in inhuman conditions where their miseries know no end. Though there are laws banning child labour, children continue to be exploited as cheap labour, because the authorities are unable to implement the laws meant to protect children from being engaged as labourers. Unfortunately the actual number of child labourers in India goes undetected. Children are forced to work in completely unregulated conditions, without adequate food, proper wages and rest, and they are subjected to physical, sexual and emotional abuse.

Loss of jobs of parents in a slowdown, the suicide of farmers, armed conflicts and the high cost of healthcare are other factors contributing to child labour.

The remedy is not a single law but a chain of them: **compulsory schooling with mid-day meals, work for the parents, strict inspection of small workshops and dhabas, and a public refusal to employ or buy from those who employ children**. A country that sends rockets to Mars cannot allow its children to break stones on the highway.

**Format points.** Title, a definition, the forms of the evil, its causes, the legal position and a concrete remedy — in about 200 words.

questions.question: Write an article on the merits and demerits of 'Polythene bags' in about 200 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**POLYTHENE BAGS — CONVENIENCE AND CATASTROPHE**

Polythene is very useful in building and construction, electronics, packaging, transport and industry. It is very easy to make — water bottles, plastic bags, pens, cups, chairs and a thousand other things come out of it cheaply. Light, strong and waterproof, a polythene bag has replaced cloth, paper and leaf in every market of India.

The main advantages of plastic materials are also the reason why plastic is such a problem. **It lasts forever and it is cheap to make.** "Lasts forever" means that it does not biodegrade. There is a floating island of plastic the size of Texas in the Pacific Ocean, and it gradually photo-degrades into tiny pieces that enter the marine food chain. Animals swallow the bags and die. Drains are choked and cities are flooded.

When polythene is burnt, the gas it gives off is very harmful to our health and environment; it weakens the ozone layer. And because most plastic is produced from oil, the world is gradually running out of the raw material itself.

Scientists are now developing plastics made from vegetable oil and other organic matter, so that the material becomes degradable and less of a problem in future. Until then the answer is the cloth bag and the steel tiffin — small habits repeated by millions.

**Format points.** A balanced article gives both sides in separate paragraphs and ends with a workable suggestion; do not write a one-sided tirade when the question asks for merits **and** demerits.

questions.question: Who is the poet of the lines 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever / Its loveliness increases, it will never / pass into nothingness, but will keep / A bower quiet for us, and a sleep / Full of sweet dreams and health, and quiet breathing'? What is the name of the poem?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poet — **John Keats**; poem — **A Thing of Beauty** (the opening lines of *Endymion*).

**Context.** These are the poem's first five lines, and they state its whole argument: beauty is permanent, its loveliness increases rather than decays, and it provides human beings with a quiet "bower", a sleep "full of sweet dreams and health, and quiet breathing". Everything that follows in the poem is an illustration of these lines — the sun, the moon, the trees, the daffodils, the clear rills and the musk-rose.

questions.question: How is a thing of beauty a joy for ever?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Because **beautiful things give us pleasure, refresh our mind and satisfy us**; a thing of beauty provides "a sleep full of sweet dreams and health and quiet breathing" to the next generation as well, and therefore such things — art, literature and nature — **must be preserved**.

**Explanation.** Keats distinguishes between the pleasure of the moment and the permanence of beauty. A beautiful object never "passes into nothingness": its loveliness "increases", and each generation finds in it the same relief from the "gloomy" days of life. That is why the poem's catalogue of natural beauties ends not with a description but with a promise of lasting joy.

questions.question: What is a bower? What does it provide for us?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** A **bower is a shadowed, sheltered place** — a quiet, shady nook under trees. It provides us **a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing**, that is, rest, peace of mind and relief from the fatigue and sadness of life.

**In the poem's words.**

> "it will never pass into nothingness, but will keep / A bower quiet for us, and a sleep / Full of sweet dreams and health, and quiet breathing."

**Explanation.** The image is of a tired traveller who finds shade and coolness after a day in the sun; beauty does the same for the mind. Keats repeats the idea in the closing lines, where each "shape of beauty" pours "a flowery band" to "bind us to the earth" and remove "the pall from our dark spirits".

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the lines 'Perhaps the Earth can teach us / as when everything seems dead / and later proves to be alive. / Now I'll count up to twelve / and you keep quiet and I will go.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **Keeping Quiet**; poet — **Pablo Neruda**.

**Context.** These are the closing lines of the poem. The poet says that the earth itself can teach us the value of stillness: it appears dead in winter and later proves to be alive. He then asks the reader to count to twelve with him and to "keep quiet" while he goes. The ending separates the poem's silence from death — it is a pause that renews life, as winter is followed by spring.

questions.question: What does the poet ask us while he counts up to twelve? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** While he counts up to twelve the poet asks us to **keep quiet and not to move our arms so much** — to stop all our activity for a moment, to give up the use of machines and engines for a short while and to keep still without speaking any language.

**Explanation.** In "Keeping Quiet" he asks for "a second of inactivity", explaining at once that he does not want total inactivity or death: "What I want should not be confused with total inactivity." His reason is stated plainly — "most of our troubles are due to our hurry and becoming rash", and a pause would break the "sadness of never understanding ourselves".

questions.question: What painful thought comes to the poet's mind and how does she drive it away? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poetess feels pain on seeing the pale, corpse-like face of her mother. There appears her **old familiar pain of childhood** in her heart: she realises that **her mother's face has become like the withered moon of the winter season**, and she feels that time and age spare none. She drives the thought away by **looking out of the car window** at the young trees and the merry children, and by smiling and saying "see you soon, amma".

**Explanation.** In Kamala Das's poem the mother dozes "open mouthed, her face ashen like that of a corpse", and the daughter's childhood fear of losing her returns. Looking out — "and looked out" — at "young trees" and "merry children" is a deliberate shift of attention from death to life, and the parting smile at the airport hides the ache.

questions.question: What does the poet say about the world of children living in a slum? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet thinks that **the map and Shakespeare had no significance for such children**. He requests that **these windows be broken and the children be moved to the day light** — to green fields, open sky and knowledge that belongs to their own world.

**Explanation.** In "An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum" Stephen Spender describes a class of "rootless weeds" for whom the map on the wall, the portrait of Shakespeare and the "lead sky" of the city are a mockery. He asks the inspector, the visitor and the governor to "break O break open till they break the town" and let the children see "green fields" and "gold sands" — the poem's appeal for a world they can actually inhabit. The chapter is now outside the current syllabus but the question survives in older sets.

questions.question: What is the 'childish longing' that the poet refers to? Why is it vain? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet is referring to the speaker's **desire to kill all the poor and put an end to their misery at one stroke**. But he realises that this desire was **vain** — it was neither feasible nor desirable. It was a childish idea.

**Explanation.** In "A Roadside Stand" Robert Frost watches the villagers waiting beside their unsold produce and says he "wonders" — the poem's word for a passing, helpless thought — whether the "requiem" for the poor might be sung at once. He then corrects himself: "I wonder how I could have been so childish". Pity that wishes people out of existence is not a remedy; the poem's real demand is that the "greedy good-doers" stop "putting the poor for a penny in the way of the city money".

questions.question: What was on sale at the roadside stand? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Wild berries, crook-necked golden squash with silver warts**, and "beauty rest in a beautiful mountain scene" were on sale at the roadside stand.

**Explanation.** In Frost's poem the hut sells whatever the poor farm produces — berries and a few gourds — set out in the hope that the cars will stop. The poet's sharp observation is that the produce is left "in the sun" and the stand is a "little house" of patches, while the polished cars "halt" only to ask for directions or to complain about the price of gas.

questions.question: What is the 'misadventure' that William Douglas speaks about? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** When Douglas was about eleven years old he began to learn swimming in the **Y.M.C.A. swimming pool**. One morning he was all alone there. A strong young man came and **picked up skinny Douglas and threw him into the deepest part of the pool**. He was **almost drowned**. He speaks of this incident as his misadventure.

**Explanation.** In "Deep Water" the boy had just gained confidence with a pair of water wings when the older boy — "a big bruiser of a boy, probably eighteen" — tossed him in "at the deep end". He went to the bottom, came up, and sank again; the terror of that moment held him for years until he hired an instructor and trained himself out of it.

questions.question: Why did Rajkumar Shukla go to meet Gandhi? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Rajkumar Shukla wanted to meet Gandhi because he wanted to **complain about the injustice of the landlord system in Bihar** — the sharecropping arrangement in Champaran that bound the peasants to grow indigo for their landlords on unfair terms.

**Explanation.** In "Indigo" Shukla is a "poor sharecropper from Champaran", "illiterate but resolute", who comes to the December 1916 session of the Indian National Congress at Lucknow to ask for the leader's help. When Gandhi tells him he has an appointment in Kanpur and engagements elsewhere, Shukla simply follows him from place to place — to Cawnpore, to Calcutta, to Patna — until Gandhi cannot avoid him.

questions.question: Why was Franz afraid when he was going to school that day? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** When the school began there was much noise and activity, and the noise could be heard in the street. **But that day there was unusual silence**, and Franz — who had not prepared his lesson on participles and feared being scolded by M. Hamel and his "great ruler" — was afraid to go in.

**Explanation.** In "The Last Lesson" Franz is already late and has prepared nothing; the unusual quiet, which he at first takes for a trick of the teacher, frightens him more than the usual din. The silence is in fact the mark of the last lesson, and the boy who dreaded a scolding ends by understanding what a whole people has lost.

questions.question: Where does the narrator Anees Jung encounter Saheb every morning? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Anees Jung encounters Saheb **searching for gold in the garbage dumps of her neighbourhood**. Saheb is one of the barefoot rag-picker boys, who can be seen searching for money, gold, silver or any other precious items in the garbage.

**Explanation.** In "Lost Spring" the author sees him "in the morning" at the dumps near her house, with a plastic bag on his shoulder, "searching for gold" in other people's waste. His name, Saheb-e-Alam, means "lord of the universe", and the gap between the name and the barefoot boy at the dump is the image the chapter is built on.

questions.question: Why do most celebrity writers despise being interviewed? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Because the interview, since its invention a little over 130 years ago, has become a **commonplace of journalism**: almost everybody reads one, and **several thousand celebrities have been interviewed over the years, some repeatedly**, so their opinion of the interview varies considerably — and mostly for the worse.

**Explanation.** In Christopher Silvester's "The Interview", taken from *The Penguin Book of Interviews*, the dislike is traced to the interview's power: a few minutes' talk is printed as a considered view, the interviewer controls what is shown, and the writer feels "wounded" by the portrait. H. G. Wells called it "an affront", Rudyard Kipling "immoral" and "a crime", and even its admirers admit it is "a necessary evil".

questions.question: Why was Sophie jealous of her brother's silence? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sophie and Geoff have nothing in common: Geoff is an **apprentice mechanic**, does not share Sophie's **wild dreams** and **speaks little**. She is jealous of his silence, and wishes he could share her fantasy about a vast world out there waiting for her.

**Explanation.** In "Going Places" Sophie imagines that Geoff's silences hide a wider experience: he travels, he listens, people tell him things. In her loneliness "she sees herself riding behind Geoff to the world of fantasy" — and she makes him the audience for the story of Danny Casey precisely because he says almost nothing about it to anyone else.

questions.question: Who was Rajkumar Shukla? How did he take Gandhi to Champaran and why? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Rajkumar Shukla was a **poor sharecropper from Champaran**. He met Gandhi in Lucknow at the December 1916 annual convention of the Indian National Congress. He had come to the Congress session **to complain about the injustice of the landlord system in Bihar**. Somebody advised him to meet Gandhi.

Gandhiji told Shukla that he had an appointment in Kanpur. He was also committed to go to other parts of India. But Shukla was determined. He accompanied Gandhi everywhere. For weeks he never left Gandhi's side. He begged Gandhi to fix a date. Gandhi was impressed by the devotion of Shukla and asked him to come to Calcutta and meet him. Months passed; Gandhi arrived in Calcutta. Shukla waited till Gandhi was free. Now it was impossible for Gandhi to avoid him. Then the two of them boarded a train for Patna in Bihar.

**Why it mattered.** The visit that began as one peasant's insistence became the Champaran campaign — the first mass movement of its kind in India — in which Gandhi gathered evidence from the sharecroppers, defied an order to leave the district, and won a settlement for the peasants.

questions.question: How did Douglas overcome his fear of water? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Fear of water held William Douglas firmly in its grip. Such fear ruined his joy of boating, fishing and swimming. He used various ways to overcome his fear, but with little success. Finally he decided to employ an instructor and learn to swim. He went to a pool and practised five days a week, an hour each day. Douglas was successful in his mission; soon he became an expert swimmer.

**What the training consisted of.** The instructor taught him to inhale and exhale in the water, to kick with his legs, and to relax and float, holding him on the end of a rope until the habit was secure. Douglas then tested himself alone — at the pool, in Lake Wentworth, and finally in the warm surf of Baja California — until the "old terror" was gone.

**The lesson he drew.** "All we have to fear is fear itself." In "Deep Water" the fear of water was conquered not by a single act of courage but by the patient repetition of small, safe actions.

questions.question: Describe Jack's art of storytelling. How does Jack narrate the story 'Should Wizard Hit Mommy'? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Jack seems to have perfected the art of story-telling. Jack has a basic tale. Each new story is a slight variation of the basic tale. There is a small creature, usually named **Roger**, in every story. It can be Roger fish, Roger squirrel or Roger chipmunk. Then there is a wise old owl and a wizard with a magic wand in every story.

Jack understands the pulse of his little daughter Jo, so he creates special effects to keep her intact. He may imitate the voice of the old wizard; he narrates the story in a way that suits the occasion. He is always full of creative enthusiasm. In this story a new animal is chosen: he is named **Roger Skunk**. He smells very bad. All little creatures keep away from him; no one plays with him. Roger goes to the wise old owl, who directs him to the wizard and tells his tragic story to him. He gives seven pennies to the wizard and becomes very happy, and makes Roger smell like a rose. Jack sticks to his version of the story and makes no change in it as desired by Jo. Jo wants the stupid mommy to be punished; she wants the wizard to smell Roger bad again. Jack doesn't relent, and makes no change in the ending.

**The tension in the story.** Jo has begun to see that a mother may be wrong, and Jack — who invented the story to comfort her — finds that his own simple tale has raised a question he cannot answer. His refusal to change the ending is both a father's authority and the end of the story's innocence. (The chapter is now outside the current syllabus.)

questions.question: What does the third level refer to? Is it a medium of getting away from the unpleasant normal life? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The third level is a **medium of escape for Charley**. He has a strange daydream wish to escape from his present worries. He wanted to escape into the past. He believed that in the old days life was peaceful. People in his grandfather's time, especially in small towns, lived a carefree life. All those charms were lost; the recent day is full of worries, wars, tension and haste.

Charley was always lost in his own thoughts. He was unaware of his surroundings. One day he found himself in the lobby of the **Roosevelt Hotel**, and another time he came up in an office building. Another day he reached the third level.

**What the third level is.** At Grand Central Station, where only two levels exist, Charley finds a corridor sloping downward into a gas-lit platform of the 1890s, with a wooden locomotive and a newsboy shouting about President Cleveland. He buys two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois — the town of his boyhood.

**Escape or delusion?** The story leaves the question open. For Charley the third level is "a waking-dream wish to escape"; whether it is a real door into the past or a symptom of his "worry" is exactly what the psychiatrist, and the reader, must decide.

questions.question: Who was Evans? What did he try? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Evans was a **thief** by profession, known to the prison staff as "Evans the Breaker". He tried to **sit an O-Level German examination in his cell** — and used the examination as the occasion to escape from prison for the fourth time.

**Explanation.** From "Evans Tries an O-Level" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus), Evans had already escaped three times, so the Governor took personal charge of the security arrangements for the examination. Evans, however, had planned everything in advance: he was examined by a bogus invigilator, and walked out of the prison disguised as one. The story is a comedy of the officials' over-confidence.

questions.question: Where did Charley want to go? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Charley wanted to go to the **third level of the Grand Central Station**, which is an **imaginary world of peace** — and from there to **Galesburg, Illinois**, the town of his boyhood.

**Explanation.** In Jack Finney's story Charley buys two tickets to Galesburg on the third-level platform for himself and his wife Louisa, because the Galesburg he sees there is "a wonderful town still" with "big old frame houses, huge lawns, and tremendous trees". His longing for it is a longing for the 1890s — a world he never actually lived in.

questions.question: Whom did the Tiger King want to marry? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The Tiger King wanted to marry a **princess from a state which possessed a large number of tigers**. His plan was to kill five or six tigers on every visit to his father-in-law's state, so that he could complete the tally of a hundred.

**Explanation.** In Kalki's story the Maharaja had killed seventy tigers in his own kingdom and the species had become extinct there. His idea of "master strategy" was therefore to marry into a state rich in tigers; he chose a princess of such a state from the three photographs placed before him, and killed ninety-nine tigers in all before the hundredth — a wooden toy — killed him.

questions.question: Who is Roger Skunk? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Roger Skunk is a **small animal** — a young skunk — who **smells very bad**, so that all the other little creatures run away from him and no one plays with him. He goes to the wizard to be given a pleasant smell.

**Explanation.** In "Should Wizard Hit Mommy?" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus) Roger is the hero of the bedtime story Jack invents for his daughter Jo. The wizard makes him smell like a rose and Roger is happy — but his mother is angry, takes him back to the wizard's hut, and makes him smell like a skunk again. Jo insists the mother should be punished; Jack refuses to change the ending, and the story becomes an argument between a father and a daughter about a mother's authority.
